# ---- L4 vs L7 at a glance ----
#                     L4 (TCP/UDP)                 L7 (HTTP)
#  decides on         5-tuple, at connect          per request, after parsing
#  sees payload       no                           yes (must terminate TLS)
#  route by path      no                           yes
#  retry a request    no                           yes (if idempotent)
#  add XFF header     no (use PROXY protocol)      yes
#  TLS                can pass through             terminates (or re-encrypts)
#  cost               microseconds                 milliseconds
#  gRPC/HTTP2         pins whole connection        balances per request
#  examples           NLB, IPVS, HAProxy tcp mode  ALB, nginx, Envoy, Traefik

# ---- nginx L7 upstream with sane failure behaviour ----
upstream api {
    least_conn;                       # adapts to slow backends; RR does not
    server 10.0.2.11:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 10.0.2.12:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 10.0.2.13:8080 backup;     # only used when the others are down
    keepalive 64;                     # pooled upstream conns (needs the two
}                                     # proxy_ directives below)

server {
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://api;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";        # required for upstream keepalive
        proxy_connect_timeout 2s;              # fail fast on a dead backend
        proxy_read_timeout   30s;              # must exceed slowest real request
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
        proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;
        # DANGER: do NOT add non_idempotent here unless you mean
        #         "retry POSTs", which can double-write.
    }
}

# ---- Consistent hashing: why it is not just "hash mod N" ----
#  hash % N   : add 1 backend to 10 -> ~90% of keys move  (cache stampede)
#  ring/Maglev: add 1 backend to 10 -> ~1/11 of keys move
upstream cache_pool {
    hash $request_uri consistent;     # nginx's consistent-hash ring
    server cache-1:11211;
    server cache-2:11211;
}

# ---- Draining: the deploy-time 502 fix ----
# Kubernetes: endpoint removal and SIGTERM race. Give the LB time to notice.
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 15"]   # >= 1 health-check interval
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45              # > preStop + longest request
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }       # deep: deps included
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }      # shallow: "am I wedged"
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 6                          # tolerant: a GC pause is not death

# Health-check anti-patterns:
#   /healthz that returns 200 unconditionally  -> LB never ejects a broken pod
#   /healthz that queries the DB every 2s      -> a DB blip ejects EVERY pod
#                                                 at once (correlated failure)

sections.title: 14. Proxies and Reverse Proxies: Headers, Timeouts, and Retries
sections.content:
A proxy is any intermediary that terminates a client connection and opens its own connection onward. The direction of trust is what distinguishes the two kinds. A forward proxy is configured by the client and acts on the client's behalf: it is how you centralise egress from a private network, enforce an allowlist of external destinations, add authentication to outbound calls, and get one audit log of everything leaving. In cloud environments, egress proxies matter because 'which of our 400 services is calling this third-party API' is otherwise unanswerable. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts on their behalf: clients think they are talking to the origin. It is the load balancer, TLS terminator, cache, rate limiter, and WAF attachment point, all in the same box. A sidecar in a service mesh is both at once - an outbound forward proxy and an inbound reverse proxy for one workload.

Because the proxy terminates the connection, the origin sees the proxy's IP as the client. Every layer of your access logging, rate limiting, and geo-based logic breaks unless the real client address is carried forward. For HTTP, the convention is X-Forwarded-For, which is a comma-separated list where each proxy appends the address it saw. The standardised replacement is the Forwarded header (RFC 7239), which also carries proto and host, though X-Forwarded-* remains far more widely deployed. The critical security property: X-Forwarded-For is client-controllable. A request that arrives at your edge already carrying an XFF header is not trustworthy, so your edge must overwrite it rather than append, and your origin must extract the client IP by counting from the right-hand side by a known number of trusted hops, or by matching against a list of trusted proxy CIDRs. Getting this wrong gives attackers free IP spoofing against your rate limiter and your audit log.

For non-HTTP traffic, or when you want to keep TLS end to end, there is no header to add - so the PROXY protocol exists: the proxy prepends a small preamble to the TCP stream declaring the original source and destination address, before any application bytes. Both ends must agree; a server expecting PROXY protocol that receives a plain connection sees garbage, and a server not expecting it that receives the preamble treats it as a malformed request. That mismatch is a classic 'everything broke the moment we enabled it on the load balancer only' incident.

Timeouts are the part people get wrong most consistently. There are at least four in a proxy hop - connect timeout, request write timeout, response read timeout, and idle keep-alive timeout - and their relationship to the client's timeout and the backend's timeouts determines whether failures are clean or produce mysterious 502s. Two rules make it tractable. First, timeouts should decrease as you go inward: the client waits longer than the edge, which waits longer than the service, which waits longer than the database. If an inner timeout exceeds an outer one, the outer gives up while the inner keeps working, and you burn capacity on results nobody will read. Second, idle keep-alive timeouts must increase as you go inward: the backend must hold an idle pooled connection open longer than the proxy will, or the proxy will reuse a socket the backend is closing at that exact moment and return a 502. AWS's ALB defaults to a 60-second idle timeout, which is why 'set the app's keepAliveTimeout to 65-75 seconds' is standard advice for Node and Go services behind an ALB.

Retries are a proxy's most dangerous feature. A retry converts a transient failure into a success, and it also converts an overloaded backend into a dead one, because retrying failed requests multiplies load exactly when there is least capacity. Three disciplines make retries safe: only retry idempotent requests (or requests carrying an idempotency key), always use exponential backoff with jitter so retries do not synchronise into a thundering herd, and enforce a retry budget - a cap such as 'retries may not exceed 10% of total requests' - so the system cannot amplify its own failure. Add circuit breaking so a backend that is failing consistently is skipped entirely for a cool-down rather than retried forever. Finally, note that nginx's proxy_next_upstream will by default retry on error and timeout, and a timeout retry on a POST is exactly the double-write hazard, which is why non_idempotent is off by default and should stay off.

sections.title: 15. NAT and Connection Tracking: The Stateful Layer Everyone Forgets
sections.content:
NAT rewrites addresses in flight. Source NAT (SNAT, and its dynamic form masquerade) rewrites the source address of outbound packets so many private hosts can share one public address; destination NAT (DNAT, and its common form port forwarding) rewrites the destination so an outside client reaching a public address is delivered to a private one. Both are inherently stateful: to un-rewrite the reply, the device must remember the translation. That memory is the connection tracking table (conntrack in Linux), and almost every surprising NAT failure is really a conntrack failure.

The mechanics of SNAT are worth stating precisely because they explain the capacity limit. When 10.0.1.4:51000 sends to 93.184.216.34:443 through a NAT with public IP 203.0.113.7, the NAT picks a free source port on its own address - say 40001 - and records the mapping. The reply arrives addressed to 203.0.113.7:40001, the NAT looks it up, rewrites the destination back to 10.0.1.4:51000, and forwards it. The uniqueness constraint is per destination: the tuple (public IP, public port, destination IP, destination port, protocol) must be unique. So a NAT with one public IP can hold roughly 64,000 simultaneous flows toward any single destination IP and port, and no more. This is exactly the documented AWS limit of 55,000 simultaneous connections per unique destination for a NAT gateway, and it is exactly the wall that a fleet of pods all polling one third-party API hits, producing intermittent connection timeouts that no application log explains. The fixes are more source addresses (more NAT gateways or more public IPs), or - better - fewer connections through connection reuse, or bypassing the NAT entirely with a VPC endpoint or a direct route.

The conntrack table itself is finite. Its size is nf_conntrack_max, sized from memory at boot, and when it fills, the kernel drops new connections and logs 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet'. On a busy Kubernetes node with many short-lived connections, this is a real ceiling, and the corresponding symptom - a small percentage of connections failing while most succeed - is maddening without the counter. Watch conntrack_count against conntrack_max as a standing metric on any node that does NAT.

Kubernetes deserves specific mention because it uses NAT far more than people realise. A Service ClusterIP is not an address that exists on any interface - it is a DNAT rule. When a pod connects to 10.96.0.10:53, kube-proxy's iptables (or IPVS, or the newer nftables backend) rules rewrite the destination to a chosen endpoint pod IP, and conntrack remembers the choice so the whole flow goes to the same pod. This is why you cannot ping a ClusterIP (there is nothing to answer ICMP, only a DNAT rule for the service's ports), and why an endpoint list change does not move existing connections. Traffic leaving the node for the outside is additionally SNATed to the node IP, which is why the destination sees the node address and why setting externalTrafficPolicy: Local exists - it preserves the client source IP by only routing to pods on the receiving node, at the cost of uneven balancing.

One famous bug is worth carrying into an interview because it demonstrates real depth: the Kubernetes five-second DNS timeout. glibc sends the A and AAAA queries for a name in parallel from the same source port, and both get SNATed at the same instant on the same node. A race in the kernel's conntrack insertion path meant one of the two entries could be lost, silently dropping one query, and glibc then waits out its five-second timeout before retrying. The mitigations that actually work are recognisable: adding the --random-fully flag to the masquerade rule to reduce port collision, using single-request-reopen in resolv.conf so the two queries use different sockets, or deploying NodeLocal DNSCache so the queries never traverse SNAT at all. Newer kernels fixed the underlying race, but the shape of the bug - 'exactly 5 seconds, only sometimes, only for DNS' - is a pattern worth recognising.

Finally, NAT breaks two things structurally. Protocols that embed IP addresses inside their payload (classic FTP, SIP, some RPC systems) need protocol-aware helpers to rewrite the payload too. And inbound connections are impossible without an explicit forward, which is why hole punching, STUN/TURN, and hairpin NAT (the trick that lets an internal host reach its own public address) exist as workarounds.

# ---- SNAT: many private hosts, one public address ----
#   10.0.1.4:51000 -> 93.184.216.34:443
#     rewritten to 203.0.113.7:40001 -> 93.184.216.34:443
#   reply to       203.0.113.7:40001 <- looked up, rewritten back to 10.0.1.4:51000
#
#   Uniqueness constraint: (natIP, natPort, dstIP, dstPort, proto)
#   => ~64k simultaneous flows per (public IP -> one dst ip:port).
#      AWS NAT Gateway documents 55,000 per unique destination.

# The rules themselves
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.0.1.0/24 -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE --random-fully
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 443 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.0.2.11:8443

# ---- conntrack is the thing that actually breaks ----
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count      # current entries
sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max        # ceiling (sized from RAM at boot)
dmesg | grep -i conntrack
# nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet   <- a % of conns fail, rest are fine

conntrack -L | head                          # live translations
conntrack -L -d 93.184.216.34 | wc -l        # how many flows to ONE destination
conntrack -E                                 # stream events (NEW/UPDATE/DESTROY)

# Alert on this ratio on every NAT/Kubernetes node:
#   nf_conntrack_count / nf_conntrack_max > 0.8

# ---- Port exhaustion signature ----
#  symptom : ~1% of outbound calls to ONE third-party API time out; the rest
#            are fine; no error in any application log; worsens with fleet size.
#  proof   : conntrack -L -d <that API> | wc -l  approaches 55k/64k
#  fixes   : (1) reuse connections (HTTP keep-alive / pooling) -- best
#            (2) more source IPs: extra NAT gateways / EIPs
#            (3) bypass NAT: VPC endpoint, direct route, or private link

# ---- Kubernetes: a ClusterIP is a DNAT rule, not an address ----
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | head
# ping 10.96.0.10          -> never works: nothing owns that IP
# curl 10.96.0.10:53       -> works: DNAT rewrites to a real pod IP
#   conntrack pins the flow to the endpoint chosen at connect time,
#   so scaling up does NOT move existing connections.

# The 5-second DNS timeout (A and AAAA race through SNAT together):
#  fix 1: --random-fully on the masquerade rule (above)
#  fix 2: per-pod resolver option so the two queries use different sockets
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - name: single-request-reopen
      - name: ndots
        value: "1"
#  fix 3: NodeLocal DNSCache -- queries never traverse SNAT at all

sections.title: 16. Firewalls, Security Groups, and the Difference Between DROP and REJECT
sections.content:
A packet filter decides, per packet, whether to allow, drop, or reject. The property that determines how usable it is in practice is statefulness. A stateless filter evaluates each packet in isolation, so if you allow inbound TCP to port 443, you must also write a rule allowing the outbound reply from port 443 to the client's ephemeral port range - and the same in reverse for outbound connections. A stateful filter tracks connections (again, conntrack), so a single rule 'allow inbound tcp/443' automatically permits the return traffic of any connection it accepted. Statefulness is why security groups feel simple and network ACLs feel painful.

On Linux, the filter is netfilter, configured historically by iptables and now by nftables. The model is hooks in the packet path, organised into tables and chains: filter (accept/drop), nat (translation), mangle (header rewriting), and raw (bypass conntrack), traversed at PREROUTING, INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT, and POSTROUTING. Two rules of thumb make reading a real ruleset possible: a packet destined for a local process goes PREROUTING then INPUT, while a packet being routed through the box goes PREROUTING, FORWARD, POSTROUTING - so if you are debugging a container host or a NAT box and looking at INPUT, you may be looking at the wrong chain entirely. Within a chain, rules are evaluated in order and the first terminating match wins, which is the opposite of how security groups work.

AWS security groups are stateful, allow-only, and evaluated as a union: there are no deny rules, every rule is a permit, and a packet is allowed if any rule in any attached group permits it. Order is irrelevant. The default posture is deny all inbound, allow all outbound - and the outbound half is worth arguing about, because unrestricted egress is how an exploited container exfiltrates data and reaches a command-and-control host. The security-group feature that most teams underuse is referencing another security group as a source: 'allow tcp/5432 from sg-app' expresses the intent (the app tier may reach the database) in a way that keeps working as instances come and go, instead of hardcoding CIDRs that drift. Network ACLs, by contrast, are stateless, ordered, support explicit deny, and operate at the subnet boundary - which makes them the right tool for a coarse, non-negotiable block (a bad CIDR, a compliance boundary) and the wrong tool for everyday service-to-service policy, because you must remember to permit ephemeral return ports (1024-65535) in the opposite direction.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is a third model with its own trap: it is additive and default-allow. A pod that no policy selects accepts all traffic. The moment any policy selects a pod for a direction, that pod becomes default-deny for that direction, and only the union of matching policies is permitted. So 'I applied a policy and nothing broke' may mean your selector matched nothing. Also note that NetworkPolicy is enforced by the CNI plugin - it is inert if your CNI does not implement it, which surprises people who applied policies on a cluster running a plugin without policy support.

The practical debugging distinction to internalise is DROP versus REJECT. A DROP discards the packet silently, so the client sits in SYN_SENT retransmitting until its connect timeout expires - typically tens of seconds. A REJECT sends back an ICMP port-unreachable or a TCP RST, so the client fails immediately with 'connection refused'. This is a diagnostic fingerprint you can read from the client alone: a fast refusal usually means the packet reached something that answered (no listener, or an explicit reject), while a long hang usually means something chose silence - a security group, a DROP rule, or a route that goes nowhere. Cloud security groups and NACLs always drop silently, which is why 'the connection just hangs' is the canonical security-group symptom. Internally, prefer REJECT on host firewalls for services that should fail fast, because a fast, honest failure is much cheaper to debug than a 30-second hang; externally, prefer DROP so you do not confirm to a scanner that the host exists.
sections.code:
# ---- Stateful vs stateless, concretely ----
#  STATEFUL  (security group, iptables with conntrack):
#     allow in tcp/443  ->  the reply is automatically permitted
#  STATELESS (network ACL):
#     allow in  tcp/443 from 0.0.0.0/0
#     allow out tcp/1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0   <- FORGET THIS AND IT HANGS

# ---- netfilter: read the right chain for the traffic's direction ----
#   to a local process : PREROUTING -> INPUT
#   routed through box : PREROUTING -> FORWARD -> POSTROUTING
#   from local process : OUTPUT -> POSTROUTING
iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers          # -v shows the HIT COUNTERS: use them
iptables -t nat -L -n -v
nft list ruleset                          # nftables equivalent

# Which rule is actually eating the packet? Watch counters move:
watch -n1 'iptables -L INPUT -n -v | head -20'

# DROP vs REJECT is a debugging signal, not a style choice:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 5432 -j DROP     # client hangs ~30-130s
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 5432 -j REJECT --reject-with tcp-reset
                                                  # client: "connection refused"

# ---- AWS security group: allow-only, stateful, unordered, union of rules ----
# GOOD: reference the source SG, not a CIDR that will drift
#   Type   Protocol Port  Source
#   HTTPS  TCP      443   0.0.0.0/0          (public ALB)
#   PgSQL  TCP      5432  sg-0app...         <- "the app tier", not an IP range
# Default: 0 inbound rules (deny all in), 1 outbound rule (allow all out).
# Restrict egress too -- unrestricted outbound is how an exploited pod
# exfiltrates data and reaches C2.

aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0abc \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[0].{In:IpPermissions,Out:IpPermissionsEgress}'

# ---- Kubernetes NetworkPolicy: ADDITIVE, and default-allow until selected ----
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny-ingress, namespace: prod }
spec:
  podSelector: {}          # every pod in the namespace...
  policyTypes: [Ingress]   # ...becomes default-deny for INGRESS only
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: api-from-gateway, namespace: prod }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: gateway } }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }
# Gotchas: (1) a pod NO policy selects allows everything;
#          (2) egress needs its own policy INCLUDING DNS to kube-dns:53,
#              or every name lookup in the namespace fails;
#          (3) enforcement is the CNI's job -- inert if your CNI lacks support.

# ---- The 60-second triage that finds 90% of "firewall" issues ----
nc -vz db.internal 5432          # refused = reached something; hang = filtered
ss -ltnp | grep 5432             # is it even listening, and on which address?
ip route get <dst>               # is there a route at all?
tcpdump -i any -nn "host <dst> and port 5432"   # do packets leave? do replies come back?
#   packets leave, nothing returns  -> filtered inbound at the far end, or
#                                      asymmetric return path

sections.title: 17. CDN and Edge Caching: Cache Keys, Control Headers, and Why Hit Ratio Is the Metric
sections.content:
A CDN is a fleet of caching reverse proxies placed close to users, usually reachable through a single anycast address so a client's packets land at the nearest point of presence automatically. It buys you four distinct things, and being able to separate them is what makes a CDN answer sound senior. First, latency: serving from 10 ms away instead of 150 ms away removes not only transfer time but every round trip in setup - TCP handshake, TLS handshake - which on a cold connection is the dominant cost. Second, offload: every cache hit is a request your origin never sees, which is capacity you do not have to provision. Third, better transport even for uncacheable content, because the client's TCP/TLS session terminates at the edge over a short, low-loss path while the edge holds warm, high-window, long-lived connections back to origin. Fourth, absorption: a distributed edge with large capacity is where volumetric DDoS traffic goes to die instead of reaching you.

The mechanism to understand deeply is the cache key. The edge stores objects under a key that by default is something like scheme plus host plus path plus query string, and a response is served to a later request only if that request computes the same key. Everything that makes caching hard is a cache-key problem. Include a per-user cookie in the key and your hit ratio collapses to zero. Include a random analytics query parameter (utm_source and friends) and every share link becomes a separate object. Exclude a header the response actually varies on and you serve the wrong content to somebody - the mobile user gets the desktop page, or worse, one user gets another's data. The Vary response header is the protocol-level way to say 'this response depends on that request header', and it is a blunt instrument: Vary: User-Agent effectively disables caching because there are millions of distinct user-agent strings. Vary: Accept-Encoding is normal and expected. The practical discipline is to normalise the key deliberately: strip tracking parameters, sort the remaining ones, cache-key only the cookies that genuinely change the response, and never cache anything authenticated without an explicit, reviewed rule.

Freshness is controlled by Cache-Control, and its directives mean specific things worth getting exactly right. max-age is how long any cache may serve the response without revalidating. s-maxage overrides max-age for shared caches only, which is the lever that lets you say 'browsers keep this 60 seconds, the CDN keeps it an hour'. public and private say whether shared caches may store it at all - private means browser only, and is what you put on authenticated responses. no-cache does not mean 'do not store'; it means 'store it, but revalidate with the origin before each reuse'. no-store is the one that means do not keep it anywhere. immutable tells the browser not even to revalidate on reload, which is correct only for content-hashed filenames. Two directives are worth deploying deliberately because they turn origin problems into non-events: stale-while-revalidate lets the edge serve a slightly stale object immediately while it refreshes in the background, so users never wait for a revalidation, and stale-if-error lets the edge keep serving stale content when the origin is down, converting a hard outage into stale-but-working.

Revalidation is how a cache checks freshness cheaply. The origin sends an ETag (an opaque version identifier) or Last-Modified; the cache later sends If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since, and the origin answers 304 Not Modified with no body. That saves bandwidth but still costs a round trip to the origin, which is why long TTLs plus versioned URLs beat short TTLs plus revalidation for static assets.

Invalidation is the hard part, and the mature answer is to avoid needing it. Give every static asset a content hash in its filename (app.9f3c2a1.js), serve it with max-age of a year and immutable, and 'invalidate' by deploying a new filename - which is instant, atomic, and free. Reserve purge for HTML and API responses, and know that purge propagation across a global edge is not instantaneous. For origin protection, two features matter: origin shield, a designated mid-tier cache that all PoPs fetch through so a cold object costs one origin request rather than one per PoP, and request collapsing (also called coalescing), where many simultaneous misses for the same key produce a single origin fetch instead of a stampede. Without collapsing, a popular object expiring at peak sends thousands of concurrent requests to your origin in the same second - the classic cache stampede. Finally, measure cache hit ratio by request and by byte, and alert on it: a deploy that accidentally adds a Set-Cookie header to static responses can silently take the hit ratio from 95% to 0% and put ten times the normal load on your origin, and hit ratio is the only metric that shows it before the origin falls over.
sections.code:
# ---- Cache-Control directives, precisely ----
#  max-age=600            any cache may serve for 600s without asking
#  s-maxage=3600          overrides max-age FOR SHARED caches (CDN) only
#  public                 shared caches may store it
#  private                browser only -- never a CDN (use for authenticated)
#  no-cache               DO store, but revalidate before every reuse
#  no-store               do not store anywhere at all
#  must-revalidate        once stale, never serve without revalidating
#  immutable              do not revalidate even on reload (hashed filenames)
#  stale-while-revalidate=60   serve stale instantly, refresh in background
#  stale-if-error=86400        keep serving stale while the origin is down

# Static asset with a content hash in the name -- the ideal case:
#   GET /static/app.9f3c2a1.js
#   Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
#   "Invalidate" by deploying a new hash. Instant, atomic, no purge API.

# HTML that must stay fresh but must survive an origin outage:
#   Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60,
#                  stale-while-revalidate=300, stale-if-error=86400

# Authenticated JSON:
#   Cache-Control: private, no-store
#   (and make sure the CDN's cache key includes the auth header, or better,
#    that the path is excluded from caching entirely)

# ---- Revalidation: 304 costs a round trip but no body ----
# Response: ETag: "a1b2c3"
# Later:    If-None-Match: "a1b2c3"   ->  HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified

# ---- Debug a hit ratio collapse ----
curl -sI https://cdn.example.com/static/app.9f3c2a1.js | \
  grep -iE 'cache-control|age|etag|vary|x-cache|cf-cache-status|set-cookie'
# age: 3400            <- object has been cached 3400s (proof of a HIT)
# x-cache: Hit from cloudfront
# set-cookie: ...      <- ANY Set-Cookie on a static response usually makes the
#                         CDN refuse to cache it. This is the #1 silent killer.
# vary: user-agent     <- effectively disables caching (millions of variants)

# Compare a cold vs warm fetch through the edge:
for i in 1 2; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "try$i ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} age=" \
       -D - https://cdn.example.com/x.js 2>/dev/null | grep -i '^age' || echo
done

# ---- The stampede, and the two features that stop it ----
#  Without request collapsing: one popular object expires at peak ->
#    5,000 simultaneous misses -> 5,000 origin requests in one second.
#  With collapsing:  1 origin request; the other 4,999 wait for it.
#  With origin shield: cold objects cost ONE origin fetch total,
#                      not one per point of presence.
#  With stale-while-revalidate: nobody ever waits for a refresh at all.

# ---- Cache key hygiene ----
#  normalise: strip utm_*/fbclid, sort remaining query params
#  key on cookies ONLY if the response genuinely varies by them
#  never cache a response whose body depends on an Authorization header
#    unless the key includes it (and think hard before doing that)

sections.title: 18. Kubernetes Networking: Pod IPs, Services, Ingress, and What Each One Is Underneath
sections.content:
Kubernetes networking is built on one model requirement: every pod gets its own IP address, and every pod can reach every other pod at that address without NAT. Everything else is an implementation of that promise plus a service abstraction on top. Knowing which piece is a real network object and which is a rule in a table is what lets you debug it.

A pod's network is a Linux network namespace. The pod's containers share it, which is why they can talk over localhost and why they cannot both bind the same port. A CNI plugin is invoked when the pod is created and is responsible for putting an interface in that namespace, assigning an address, and making the address routable. The plugins differ in how they make it routable, and the difference is operationally significant. Overlay plugins encapsulate pod traffic in VXLAN or GENEVE so it can cross any underlying network - simple to deploy, works anywhere, costs you MTU (that 50-byte VXLAN header) and a little CPU. Routed plugins put pod CIDRs into the real routing table, often via BGP, so packets are native with no encapsulation - faster and easier to trace, but the underlying network has to cooperate. Cloud-native plugins like the AWS VPC CNI give each pod a real VPC address on a shared ENI, which means security groups and VPC flow logs apply to pods directly, at the cost of consuming VPC address space fast and hitting per-instance ENI and IP limits. A team that chose /28 subnets and then adopted the VPC CNI runs out of addresses, and the failure looks like pods stuck in ContainerCreating.

A Service is not a proxy process and mostly not a thing that exists on the network. A ClusterIP is a virtual address that lives only as a rule: kube-proxy programs iptables (default), IPVS, or the newer nftables backend on every node so that packets to that IP and port are DNATed to one of the ready endpoint pod IPs, with conntrack pinning the flow. That is why ping to a ClusterIP fails while curl to its port works, why a Service with no ready endpoints gives connection refused or timeouts rather than a helpful error, and why existing connections do not rebalance when you scale up. A headless Service (clusterIP: None) skips all of that and simply returns the pod IPs as DNS A records, which is what stateful sets and client-side load balancers want. NodePort adds a port on every node that DNATs into the same machinery, and a LoadBalancer Service asks the cloud provider to point a real external load balancer at those node ports (or, with newer controllers, directly at pod IPs).

Ingress and the Gateway API are a different layer: they configure an actual L7 proxy (nginx, Envoy, HAProxy, or a cloud ALB) that terminates HTTP, matches host and path rules, and forwards to Services. An Ingress resource is data; the ingress controller is the thing that does the work; if no controller is installed, your Ingress objects do nothing at all, silently.

DNS inside the cluster is CoreDNS, reachable at the kube-dns Service address, and it resolves service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Two behaviours cause most cluster DNS incidents. The first is the ndots:5 amplification described in the DNS section - external lookups get tried against every search domain first, multiplying query volume by four or five. The second is that CoreDNS is itself a pod behind a ClusterIP, so a DNS outage is often really a conntrack, kube-proxy, or NetworkPolicy problem: if you apply a default-deny egress policy in a namespace and forget to allow UDP and TCP port 53 to the kube-dns pods, every name lookup in that namespace fails, and the symptom appears in a hundred unrelated applications at once.

Finally, know how the source IP behaves, because it drives both security rules and debugging. Pod-to-pod traffic inside the cluster preserves the source pod IP. Traffic leaving the cluster is usually SNATed to the node IP. Traffic entering through a NodePort or LoadBalancer with the default externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster gets SNATed to the receiving node so it can be forwarded to a pod on another node - which destroys the client IP. Setting externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves the client IP by refusing to forward across nodes, at the cost of uneven balancing and requiring the load balancer to health check node-local endpoint availability. That trade - client IP fidelity versus even distribution - is a common design question.
sections.code:
# ---- What is real, and what is just a rule ----
#  pod IP        real: an interface in a network namespace, routable
#  ClusterIP     NOT real: a DNAT rule programmed by kube-proxy on every node
#  NodePort      a port on every node that DNATs into the same rules
#  LoadBalancer  a cloud LB pointed at node ports (or directly at pod IPs)
#  Ingress       data only -- inert unless a controller (nginx/Envoy) reads it

kubectl get endpointslices -n prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
# EMPTY endpoints is the #1 "my service is down": selector mismatch or
# readiness failing. Check this BEFORE touching the network.

kubectl get svc api -n prod -o wide
kubectl describe svc api -n prod | grep -A3 Endpoints

# ---- Debug from inside the cluster, not from your laptop ----
kubectl run netshoot --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
  # inside:
  dig +short api.prod.svc.cluster.local
  dig +short @10.96.0.10 api.prod.svc.cluster.local
  curl -sv http://api.prod.svc.cluster.local:8080/healthz
  curl -sv http://10.1.4.23:8080/healthz     # pod IP directly: bypasses the
                                             # Service, isolating kube-proxy
  nc -vz api.prod.svc.cluster.local 8080

# Layer isolation, in order:
#   pod IP works, ClusterIP does not   -> kube-proxy / conntrack / endpoints
#   ClusterIP works, DNS does not      -> CoreDNS or an egress NetworkPolicy
#   in-cluster works, Ingress does not -> ingress controller, LB, or TLS

# ---- kube-proxy rules on a node ----
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | grep 10.96.0.10
ipvsadm -Ln                                 # if the cluster uses IPVS mode
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy --tail=50

# ---- DNS: the ndots trap and the egress-policy trap ----
kubectl exec -it mypod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
# search prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# options ndots:5      <- "api.example.com" is tried 4 times before it resolves

# If you apply ANY default-deny egress policy, you MUST re-allow DNS or
# every lookup in the namespace fails at once:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-dns, namespace: prod }
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } }
          podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } }
      ports:
        - { protocol: UDP, port: 53 }
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }     # TCP too: large answers fall back to it

# ---- Client source IP: pick your trade-off explicitly ----
# externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster (default)
#   even balancing, extra hop, client IP is SNATed away
# externalTrafficPolicy: Local
#   client IP preserved, no extra hop, but traffic only goes to pods on the
#   receiving node -> imbalance if pods are unevenly spread across nodes
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local

sections.title: 19. A Layered Debugging Method, and curl as a Latency Profiler
sections.content:
Network debugging goes wrong when people start guessing. The method that works is bisection down the layer stack, asking one falsifiable question at a time and refusing to move on until each is answered. The order is fixed because each layer depends on the one below it.

First: does the name resolve, and to what? Use getent hosts to see what the application's resolver returns and dig to see what DNS says, because a difference between them is itself the answer. Second: is the address reachable at all? A ping tells you something, but ICMP is frequently deprioritised or blocked, so an unanswered ping proves nothing - use a TCP probe to the actual port instead. Third: does a TCP connection establish? nc -vz or curl with a short connect timeout distinguishes refused (RST came back, so the packet arrived and nothing was listening) from timed out (silence, so something dropped it). Fourth: does TLS complete, and does the certificate validate for the name you used? Fifth: does the application answer, and with what status and how fast? Only after all five do you open a packet capture, because a capture is expensive to collect and read and usually confirms what the cheaper probes already told you.

The single most useful tool in that sequence is curl with a write-out format, because it decomposes one request into its phases and tells you which one is slow. The timing variables are cumulative offsets from the start of the request, not durations, so you get the duration of each phase by subtracting the previous one. time_namelookup is DNS. time_connect minus time_namelookup is the TCP handshake, which is essentially one network round trip and therefore a direct measurement of RTT. time_appconnect minus time_connect is the TLS handshake, roughly one more round trip on TLS 1.3 and two on 1.2, plus signature work. time_starttransfer minus time_pretransfer is the server's think time - the interval where the request has been fully sent and you are waiting for the first response byte, which is exactly what you should be comparing against the server's own latency metric. time_total minus time_starttransfer is body transfer, which is where bandwidth and MTU problems live.

Reading that breakdown converts a vague 'the API is slow' into a specific accusation. Slow namelookup only on the first request means cold DNS or a search-domain amplification problem. A connect time far above the expected RTT means SYN retransmission - something is dropping packets, and the classic value to recognise is roughly one second, then three, then seven, matching Linux's exponential SYN retry backoff. A large appconnect means TLS cost: an oversized certificate chain, a slow OCSP fetch on the client, or a server doing RSA rather than ECDSA signatures. A large starttransfer with a small total means the backend is thinking - that is not a network problem and you should say so. A small starttransfer with a huge total means the body is transferring slowly, which points at bandwidth, congestion, or an MTU black hole.

Two more things make curl decisive rather than merely informative. --resolve pins a hostname to a specific address for that request while keeping the Host header, the SNI, and full certificate validation intact, so you can test one specific backend or a new load balancer before DNS points at it - which is far better than curling the IP and adding -k to work around the certificate mismatch you just created. And running the same request twice on one command line shows whether connection reuse is working, because num_connects will be 1 then 0.

A final discipline: always test from the right place. The client's laptop, a pod in the same namespace, a node in the same subnet, and a bastion outside the VPC are four different vantage points, and the layer that fails often depends on where you stand. Reproducing from inside the cluster or inside the VPC is usually what localises a problem to a security group, a NetworkPolicy, or a route.
sections.code:
# ---- The bisect, in order. Do not skip a step. ----
# 1. name
getent hosts api.example.com          # what the APP will get (NSS + /etc/hosts)
dig +short api.example.com            # what DNS says
# 2. reachability (ICMP may be blocked -- prefer a TCP probe)
ping -c3 api.example.com
nc -vz -w3 api.example.com 443
# 3. TCP -- does the handshake complete, and how long does it take?
curl -s -o /dev/null --connect-timeout 3 -w 'connect=%{time_connect} ip=%{remote_ip}\n' \
     https://api.example.com
# 4. TLS
echo | openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com
# 5. HTTP
curl -sv https://api.example.com/healthz
# 6. only now: packets
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'host api.example.com and port 443'

# ---- curl as a latency profiler (values are CUMULATIVE offsets) ----
cat > /tmp/curl-fmt.txt <<'EOF'
     dns:  %{time_namelookup}s
 connect:  %{time_connect}s
     tls:  %{time_appconnect}s
pretransf:  %{time_pretransfer}s
    ttfb:  %{time_starttransfer}s
   total:  %{time_total}s
  status:  %{http_code}   http %{http_version}   ip %{remote_ip}
connects:  %{num_connects}   redirects %{num_redirects}
    size:  %{size_download} bytes  @ %{speed_download} B/s
EOF
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "@/tmp/curl-fmt.txt" https://api.example.com/v1/orders

#   dns:       0.031   <- resolution
#   connect:   0.078   -> 0.078-0.031 = 47ms  TCP handshake  == ~1 RTT
#   tls:       0.135   -> 0.135-0.078 = 57ms  TLS handshake
#   ttfb:      0.612   -> 0.612-0.135 = 477ms SERVER THINK TIME  <- the culprit
#   total:     0.640   -> 0.640-0.612 = 28ms  body transfer

# ---- Reading the shape ----
#  connect ~= 1.0s / 3.0s / 7.0s   -> SYN retransmits: packets are being dropped
#  connect >> expected RTT         -> loss, or a distant/wrong endpoint
#  tls large                       -> fat cert chain, RSA vs ECDSA, OCSP fetch
#  ttfb large, total ~= ttfb       -> backend is slow. NOT a network problem.
#  ttfb small, total huge          -> bandwidth, congestion, or PMTU black hole
#  dns large on first call only    -> cold cache / ndots search amplification

# ---- Pin the backend without breaking TLS validation ----
curl -v --resolve api.example.com:443:10.0.5.20 https://api.example.com/healthz
#   keeps Host + SNI + cert checking. Far better than "curl https://10.0.5.20 -k".
curl --connect-to api.example.com:443:canary.internal:443 https://api.example.com/

# ---- Is keep-alive working? ----
curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'connects=%{num_connects}\n' \
     https://api.example.com/a https://api.example.com/b
# 1 then 0  -> reused.   1 then 1 -> a new handshake per request: find out why.

# ---- Loop it to see variance, not one lucky sample ----
for i in $(seq 20); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_connect} %{time_starttransfer} %{http_code}\n' \
       https://api.example.com/healthz
done | sort -n | tail -5      # the tail is where the incident lives

sections.title: 20. ss, traceroute, and mtr: Sockets and Paths
sections.content:
Three tools cover the space between 'the socket on this host' and 'the path between two hosts', and each answers a question the others cannot.

ss is the socket statistics tool, and it replaced netstat because it reads the kernel's socket tables over a netlink socket instead of parsing /proc line by line - on a host with a hundred thousand connections, netstat takes seconds and ss takes milliseconds. Learn four invocations and you will cover most of what you need. ss -s prints a one-screen summary of totals by state, which is your first look at 'is this a connection-count problem'. ss -ltnp lists listening TCP sockets numerically with the owning process, which answers 'is it even listening, and on which address' - and the answer '127.0.0.1' rather than '0.0.0.0' is the single most common cause of a service being unreachable from outside its container or host. ss -tan with a state filter and a destination filter lets you count exactly what you care about, such as how many TIME-WAIT or CLOSE-WAIT sockets exist toward one peer. And ss -ti dumps the kernel's internal TCP state per connection - RTT and its variance, congestion window, slow-start threshold, retransmit counters, whether window scaling was negotiated - which is how you distinguish 'the network is lossy' from 'the application is slow' without a packet capture.

The Recv-Q and Send-Q columns mean different things depending on socket state, and this trips people up constantly. On an established socket, Recv-Q is bytes received by the kernel that the application has not read yet - a persistently non-zero Recv-Q means your application is not reading fast enough - and Send-Q is bytes written by the application that the kernel has not had acknowledged, so a large Send-Q means the peer or the network is not draining them. On a listening socket, the same columns are repurposed: Recv-Q is the current number of completed connections waiting in the accept queue and Send-Q is the maximum size of that queue.

traceroute maps the path. It works by exploiting TTL: it sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on, and each router that decrements the TTL to zero must return an ICMP time-exceeded message revealing its address. On Linux the default probes are UDP packets to high ports, which many firewalls drop, so a traceroute that dies halfway across the internet is usually a filtering artefact rather than a broken path. Use -I for ICMP probes or, most usefully for debugging a real service, -T to send TCP SYNs to the actual destination port, because that follows the same path and passes the same firewall rules as your real traffic. The most important interpretive rule: asterisks at an intermediate hop do not mean packet loss. Routers deprioritise or rate-limit the generation of ICMP errors as a matter of policy, so a middle hop can show 100% loss while traffic passes through it perfectly. Only loss that persists to the final hop, and to every hop after a certain point, is real.

mtr combines traceroute and ping: it runs the probes continuously and shows per-hop loss and latency statistics that accumulate over time, which is what you actually want, because a single traceroute is one sample of a path that may be load-balanced across several routes. Run it with enough cycles to be meaningful (a hundred is a reasonable default), use --tcp with the real port so you are measuring the path your traffic takes, and read it with the same discipline: find the first hop where loss appears and stays for every subsequent hop including the last. Latency that jumps at one hop and stays elevated is a real change (a long link, or congestion); latency that spikes at one hop and returns to normal afterwards is that router being slow at answering probes, not slow at forwarding. Also expect asymmetry: mtr shows you the forward path only, and the return path can be completely different, so when a result looks impossible, run mtr from the far end too.
sections.code:
# ---- ss: the four invocations that cover most incidents ----
ss -s                            # totals by state, per protocol
ss -ltnp                         # LISTENING tcp, numeric, with process
# LISTEN 0 4096 127.0.0.1:8080  users:(("app",pid=812,fd=6))
#              ^^^^^^^^^ bound to loopback: unreachable from anywhere else

ss -tanp state established dst 10.0.7.9         # who am I talking to
ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l                 # TIME_WAIT pressure
ss -tan state close-wait | wc -l                # >0 and growing = fd leak
ss -tunap                                        # tcp+udp, all, numeric, process
ss -tan '( dport = :5432 or sport = :5432 )'     # filter expressions work too

# Per-connection kernel TCP internals (no packet capture needed):
ss -ti dst 10.0.7.9
#  cubic wscale:7,7 rto:212 rtt:5.4/1.1 mss:1448 cwnd:10 ssthresh:7
#  bytes_sent:44M bytes_retrans:1.9M retrans:0/1204 lastsnd:12 lastrcv:8
#   rtt:5.4/1.1     smoothed RTT / variance in ms
#   retrans:0/1204  1204 retransmits over the connection's life -> real loss
#   cwnd:10 pinned low with a high ssthresh -> repeated congestion events
#   no "wscale" at all -> window scaling missing: throughput capped at 64KB/RTT

# ---- Recv-Q / Send-Q mean DIFFERENT things per state ----
#  ESTABLISHED  Recv-Q = bytes the app has not read()   (app too slow)
#               Send-Q = bytes not yet ACKed by peer    (network/peer too slow)
#  LISTEN       Recv-Q = connections waiting in the accept queue
#               Send-Q = max accept queue size (the effective backlog)

# ---- traceroute: use the protocol and port your traffic actually uses ----
traceroute api.example.com               # Linux default: UDP high ports (often filtered)
traceroute -I api.example.com            # ICMP probes
sudo traceroute -T -p 443 api.example.com  # TCP SYN to the REAL port  <- best
traceroute -n api.example.com            # skip reverse DNS (much faster)

#  4  10.0.0.9    1.2 ms
#  5  * * *                <- NOT loss: this router just rate-limits ICMP
#  6  203.0.113.1  8.9 ms  <- traffic clearly passed through hop 5 fine

# ---- mtr: the one to actually run ----
mtr -rwzbc 100 api.example.com                  # report, wide, ASN, both, 100 cycles
sudo mtr -rwzbc 100 --tcp --port 443 api.example.com

# HOST                     Loss%  Snt   Last   Avg  Best  Wrst StDev
# 1. gateway                0.0%  100    0.9   1.0   0.8   2.1   0.2
# 5. core2.isp.net         42.0%  100   14.2  14.9  13.8  22.0   1.1   <- ICMP
#                                                                       rate limit
# 6. peer.example.net       0.0%  100   15.1  15.4  14.9  19.2   0.6   <- proof:
#                                                                       hop 5 fine
# 9. api.example.com        7.0%  100   88.4  92.1  86.0 210.3  18.7   <- REAL
#
#  Rule: loss is real only if it persists at EVERY hop from that point on,
#        and especially at the final hop.
#  Rule: mtr measures the FORWARD path. Run it from the other end too --
#        the return path is frequently different.

sections.title: 21. tcpdump: Capturing and Actually Reading Packets
sections.content:
A packet capture is the ground truth, and it is the tool you reach for when the cheaper probes disagree with each other or with the application's own account of events. The discipline is to capture narrowly and read purposefully, because an unfiltered capture on a busy host produces gigabytes of noise and can itself affect the machine.

The capture command has four parts worth setting deliberately. The interface: -i any works on Linux and captures across all interfaces (using a cooked-capture link type that hides Ethernet headers), while naming a specific interface gives you real link-layer detail and less noise. Name resolution: always use -nn, which disables both hostname and port-name lookups - without it, tcpdump issues DNS queries while you are debugging DNS, which is both slow and confusing. A filter: the BPF expression is compiled into the kernel, so filtering costs almost nothing and is how you keep a capture small enough to read. And an exit condition: -c to stop after N packets, or -w to a file plus a time limit, so you never leave a capture running on a production box by accident. Modern tcpdump defaults its snaplen to the full packet, so the old habit of adding -s0 is no longer needed, though it is harmless.

Write to a file for anything non-trivial and read it back, ideally in Wireshark, which reassembles streams, marks retransmissions and duplicate ACKs, and can follow a TCP conversation. Reading in the terminal is fine for confirming a hypothesis; reading in Wireshark is how you discover one.

The filter language is worth a little memorisation because it pays off constantly. host, net, port, src, dst and their combinations with and/or/not cover most cases. The powerful extension is byte-offset matching: tcp[tcpflags] gives you the flags byte, so you can capture only SYNs, only RSTs, or only connection setup and teardown - which is exactly what you want when investigating why connections are failing, because it filters out all the payload. A capture of only SYN and RST packets on a busy service is small, fast, and answers 'who is refusing whom' immediately.

Reading tcpdump's output, the flags in brackets are the vocabulary: [S] is SYN, [S.] is SYN-ACK (the dot means ACK is also set), [.] is a bare ACK, [P.] is push plus ACK (data), [F.] is FIN plus ACK, and [R] or [R.] is a reset. From those alone you can classify a failure in seconds. Repeated [S] from the client with no [S.] coming back means the SYN is not being answered - a firewall drop, a missing route, or a dead host; note the retry spacing of roughly 1, 3, 7 seconds. An immediate [R] in response to a [S] means active refusal - nothing listening, or a reject rule. Handshake completes and then a [R] arrives from a middlebox after a period of silence means an idle timeout on a NAT or load balancer. The same sequence number appearing repeatedly from the sender with increasing time gaps means retransmission, which means packets are being lost.

Two capture strategies deserve to be named. First, capture on both ends simultaneously. The most valuable evidence in a networking incident is 'the client sent it and the server never saw it', and you can only establish that with two captures. It immediately partitions the problem into 'lost in the network' versus 'received and ignored by the application'. Second, for a problem that happens rarely, use a ring buffer: -W and -C let tcpdump rotate through a fixed set of files of bounded size, so you can leave it running for hours and still have the packets from the minute the incident occurred without filling the disk. Pair that with -G for time-based rotation. Finally, be aware of what a capture does not show: tcpdump taps below the application and, on modern NICs, may show you segments before hardware offloads have split them, so a single 'packet' of 40 KB in your capture is TSO/GRO coalescing, not a jumbo frame on the wire.
sections.code:
# ---- Capture narrowly, always with -nn, always with an exit condition ----
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -c 200 'host 10.0.7.9 and port 5432'
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -w /tmp/cap.pcap 'host 10.0.7.9 and tcp port 443'
#   -nn  no name AND no port resolution (never do DNS while debugging DNS)
#   -c   stop after N packets     -w  write pcap for Wireshark
#   -e   show link-layer (MAC) headers    -A/-X  ascii / hex payload
#   modern tcpdump already captures full packets: -s0 is no longer needed

# Connection setup and teardown ONLY -- tiny, and answers most questions:
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-rst|tcp-fin) != 0'
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0'      # who is resetting?

# Other filters worth knowing:
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'arp'                          # L2 / failover
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'udp port 53'                  # DNS
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'icmp'                         # PMTU, unreachables
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'net 10.0.0.0/8 and not port 22'
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn 'host 10.0.7.9' -A | grep -i '^Host:'   # HTTP/1 only

# ---- Reading the flags ----
#  [S]   SYN            [S.]  SYN-ACK       [.]  plain ACK
#  [P.]  PSH+ACK (data) [F.]  FIN+ACK       [R]/[R.]  RESET

# 10.0.1.4.51000 > 10.0.7.9.443: Flags [S], seq 129384, win 62727
# 10.0.1.4.51000 > 10.0.7.9.443: Flags [S], seq 129384, win 62727    (+1.0s)
# 10.0.1.4.51000 > 10.0.7.9.443: Flags [S], seq 129384, win 62727    (+3.0s)
#   -> SYNs unanswered at 1s/3s/7s: DROPPED. Firewall, SG, or no route.

# 10.0.7.9.443 > 10.0.1.4.51000: Flags [R.], seq 1, ack 1
#   -> immediate reset: nothing listening, or an explicit REJECT rule.

# ...handshake ok, 240s of silence...
# 10.0.7.9.443 > 10.0.1.4.51000: Flags [R.]
#   -> a NAT/LB dropped the idle flow's state. Lower keepalive below its timeout.

# same seq re-sent with growing gaps -> retransmission -> real packet loss

# ---- Capture on BOTH ends at once: this is the high-value move ----
# client: tcpdump -i any -nn -w /tmp/client.pcap 'host SERVER and port 443'
# server: tcpdump -i any -nn -w /tmp/server.pcap 'host CLIENT and port 443'
#   client sent, server never saw it -> lost in the network / filtered
#   server saw it, app never logged  -> accept queue, app bug, or wrong vhost

# ---- Long-running capture for a rare event, without filling the disk ----
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -w /tmp/ring.pcap -C 100 -W 20 'port 443'
#   -C 100  rotate every 100 MB    -W 20  keep 20 files (2 GB ceiling)
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -w /tmp/hourly-%Y%m%d-%H%M.pcap -G 3600 -W 24 'port 443'

# ---- Read it back ----
tcpdump -nn -r /tmp/cap.pcap | head -50
tcpdump -nn -r /tmp/cap.pcap 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0'
tshark -r /tmp/cap.pcap -q -z conv,tcp          # per-conversation byte/packet totals
tshark -r /tmp/cap.pcap -Y 'tcp.analysis.retransmission' | wc -l
tshark -r /tmp/cap.pcap -Y 'http.response.code >= 500'

# ---- Caveat: what you see may not be what the wire saw ----
# NIC offloads (TSO/GRO/LRO) coalesce segments before tcpdump taps them, so a
# 40KB "packet" in your capture is an offload artefact, not a jumbo frame.
ethtool -k eth0 | grep -E 'segmentation|offload'

sections.title: 22. A Catalogue of Production Network Failures (and Their Fingerprints)
sections.content:
Interviews at the senior level converge on the same question in different costumes: have you actually debugged this, and can you recognise a failure from its symptom? This section is the pattern library. Each entry pairs a symptom you can observe from outside with the mechanism underneath and the fix that addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

Intermittent 502s during and after every deploy. The mechanism is almost always a race between endpoint removal and process termination: the load balancer is still forwarding to a pod that has already begun shutting down, or the backend closed a pooled keep-alive connection at the instant the proxy sent a request onto it. The fix is a drain sequence - fail readiness first, keep serving for at least one health-check interval (a preStop sleep), then shut down gracefully - plus the timeout ordering rule that the backend's idle keep-alive timeout must exceed the load balancer's.

A small, steady percentage of requests to one external API time out, and it gets worse as you scale up. This is SNAT port exhaustion. Every pod's outbound connection consumes a port on the NAT's public address, the tuple must be unique per destination, and the ceiling is tens of thousands per destination IP and port. The proof is counting conntrack entries to that destination. The fix is connection reuse first (an HTTP client with a properly sized keep-alive pool almost always makes this vanish), then more source addresses, then bypassing NAT with a private endpoint.

DNS lookups that take exactly five seconds, sometimes. That precise number is glibc's resolver timeout, and in Kubernetes it classically indicated the conntrack race where parallel A and AAAA queries collided during SNAT. Fixes: single-request-reopen, NodeLocal DNSCache, --random-fully on the masquerade rule, or a newer kernel. The general lesson - suspiciously round timeout values are the client's timer, not the network's latency - transfers to every stack.

TLS handshake succeeds and small responses work, but large responses hang. PMTU black hole. Some hop has a smaller MTU and the ICMP fragmentation-needed message is being filtered, so the sender never learns to send smaller segments. Confirm with ping and the do-not-fragment bit at descending sizes; fix by clamping MSS on the SYN rather than depending on ICMP.

Everything worked until traffic doubled, and now a fraction of connections fail with no application-side error. Look at the counters, in this order: accept queue overflows (nstat ListenOverflows), conntrack table usage against its max, NIC drops in ip -s link, and ephemeral port availability. All four are silent failures that appear only in counters, which is exactly why they should be dashboards rather than ad-hoc commands.

CLOSE_WAIT sockets accumulating without bound. Not a network problem at all: the peer closed, and your application never called close on the descriptor. It ends in file-descriptor exhaustion and an unrelated-looking crash. Find the owning process with ss -tanp and fix the leak in the client library or pool.

A certificate expired despite automated renewal. Almost always the renewal wrote a new file and no process reloaded it, or one node in a fleet was missed. Monitor the certificate the server actually serves, over the network, per endpoint, rather than the file on disk - and alert with weeks of headroom, not days.

One service's failure takes down four unrelated services. Retry amplification. A failing dependency causes retries, retries multiply load, the multiplied load exhausts a shared resource - a connection pool, the conntrack table, a thread pool - and the failure spreads. The controls are a retry budget, exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breaking, and separate connection pools per dependency so one slow dependency cannot consume all the capacity.

A CDN's cache hit ratio drops to near zero after a deploy and the origin buckles. Something changed the cache key or the cacheability: a new Set-Cookie on static responses, a new Vary header, or a tracking query parameter that is now part of the key. Alert on hit ratio directly; it is a leading indicator that fires before origin load does.

And the classic pair that closes most incident reviews: it works from my laptop but not from the cluster, and it works by IP but not by name. The first is a vantage-point problem - security group, NetworkPolicy, route, or egress proxy - and is resolved by reproducing from inside the affected network namespace. The second is a resolution problem, and the discriminator is getent versus dig: if dig succeeds and the application fails, the answer is in nsswitch, /etc/hosts, the container's resolv.conf, or a client library that caches resolutions for the process lifetime.
sections.code:
# ---- Fingerprint -> mechanism -> fix ----
#
# 502s on every deploy
#   -> LB still forwarding to a terminating pod, or keep-alive close race
#   -> preStop sleep >= 1 health-check interval; backend idle timeout > LB's
#
# ~1% timeouts to ONE external API, worse at scale
#   -> SNAT port exhaustion (unique tuple per destination, ~55-64k ceiling)
#   -> conntrack -L -d <api> | wc -l   ;  fix with keep-alive pooling first
#
# DNS latency of EXACTLY 5.000s, intermittently
#   -> glibc resolver timeout; classic k8s conntrack race on parallel A/AAAA
#   -> single-request-reopen | NodeLocal DNSCache | --random-fully
#
# TLS connects, small responses fine, large responses hang
#   -> PMTU black hole (ICMP frag-needed filtered)
#   -> ping -M do -s 1472 / 1422 / 1372 ; then clamp MSS on the SYN
#
# p99 spikes but the service's own timers look clean
#   -> accept queue overflow: time is spent in the kernel, before accept()
#   -> nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows ; raise somaxconn AND listen(backlog)
#
# a % of new connections fail, most succeed, node is busy
#   -> conntrack table full
#   -> nf_conntrack_count vs _max ; dmesg | grep conntrack
#
# CLOSE_WAIT grows without bound
#   -> application never close()d the fd. Not a network problem.
#   -> ss -tanp state close-wait  ; fix the leak; watch for EMFILE next
#
# "connection reset by peer" on long-idle pooled connections
#   -> NAT/LB dropped idle flow state; next packet has nowhere to go
#   -> keepalive (or app-level ping) BELOW the device's idle timeout
#
# cert expired despite automation
#   -> renewed on disk, never reloaded; or one node missed
#   -> monitor the SERVED chain over the network, alert at 21+ days
#
# one dependency's blip becomes a multi-service outage
#   -> retry amplification exhausting a shared pool
#   -> retry budget + jittered backoff + circuit breaker + per-dep pools
#
# CDN hit ratio collapses after a deploy
#   -> Set-Cookie on static, a new Vary, or a tracking param in the key
#   -> alert on hit ratio; normalise the cache key
#
# "works from my laptop, not from the cluster"
#   -> vantage point: SG / NetworkPolicy / route / egress proxy
#   -> reproduce from inside: kubectl run netshoot --rm -it ...
#
# "works by IP, not by name"
#   -> getent hosts X  vs  dig +short X   -- the disagreement IS the answer

# ---- The counters that should be dashboards, not ad-hoc commands ----
nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops TcpExtTCPSynRetrans
nstat -az TcpRetransSegs TcpOutRsts
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max
ip -s link show eth0 | sed -n '3,6p'      # RX/TX errors, dropped, overrun
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -iE 'drop|discard|error|no_buffer'
ss -s
netstat -su | grep -i 'receive buffer errors'

# ---- A 5-minute incident script worth having in the runbook ----
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
T=${1:?usage: net-triage.sh host[:port]}
HOST=${T%%:*}; PORT=${T#*:}; [ "$PORT" = "$HOST" ] && PORT=443
echo "== resolution ==";  getent hosts "$HOST"; dig +short "$HOST"
echo "== route ==";       ip route get "$(dig +short "$HOST" | head -1)"
echo "== tcp ==";         nc -vz -w3 "$HOST" "$PORT"
echo "== timings ==";     curl -s -o /dev/null \
  -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} conn=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total} code=%{http_code}\n' \
  "https://$HOST/" || true
echo "== cert ==";         echo | openssl s_client -connect "$HOST:$PORT" \
  -servername "$HOST" 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -enddate
echo "== path ==";         mtr -rwzbc 20 "$HOST" 2>/dev/null | tail -8

interviewQA.q: Walk me through everything that happens when a user's browser requests https://api.example.com/orders and the service runs behind a load balancer in a VPC.
interviewQA.a: I would narrate it as round trips and hand-offs. First resolution: the browser and OS caches are checked, then the stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which on a miss walks root, then .com, then the authoritative servers for example.com; the answer here is typically a CNAME to a load balancer name, then A records, each cached for its TTL. With an address in hand the browser opens TCP - SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, one round trip - to the load balancer, not to my service. Then TLS: on 1.3 that is one more round trip, during which the client sends SNI so the load balancer picks the right certificate and ALPN so both sides agree on h2 or http/1.1; the load balancer proves it holds the private key for a certificate whose SAN covers api.example.com and that chains to a trusted root. Then the HTTP request goes over that connection. The load balancer, being L7, terminates the connection, parses the request, appends the client address to X-Forwarded-For, picks a backend by least-outstanding-requests among the ones passing health checks, and sends the request over a pooled keep-alive connection to a target. Inside the VPC that target might be a pod, in which case the packet is DNATed by kube-proxy rules to a pod IP and conntrack pins the flow. The application answers; the response goes back up the same path; the browser renders and reuses the connection for subsequent requests. Cold-cache total before the first byte: roughly DNS plus one RTT for TCP plus one for TLS plus one for the request, so about four round trips, and every performance feature in this stack - keep-alive, session resumption, CDN edge termination, QUIC - exists to delete one of them.
followUps: Which of those round trips disappear on the second request, and which disappear only on a second page load?
Where would you put a CDN in that path, and which of those steps would it change?
The load balancer returns a 502 for one request in a thousand. Where do you look first?

interviewQA.q: Why does TCP need a three-way handshake? Would two messages not be enough?
interviewQA.a: Two things must happen before data can flow, and they need three messages. First, TCP is full duplex and each direction has its own sequence numbering, so both sides must send an initial sequence number and have it acknowledged - that is SYN with the client's ISN, SYN-ACK carrying the server's ISN plus an acknowledgement of the client's, and ACK acknowledging the server's. Two messages would leave the server's sequence number unacknowledged. Second, the third packet proves the client can actually receive traffic at the source address it claimed. Without that proof, anyone could send SYNs with forged source addresses and force the server to allocate connection state, which is exactly the SYN flood. That is also why initial sequence numbers are randomised rather than starting at zero - it makes off-path injection and confusion with segments from a previous connection on the same four-tuple much harder. It is worth adding that Linux does have TCP Fast Open, which lets a client send data in the SYN using a cookie from a previous connection, so the round trip can be elided for repeat clients, but it is not widely deployed because middleboxes mishandle it.
followUps: What happens on the server between the SYN arriving and your application calling accept?
How does the kernel defend the SYN queue under a flood, and what does that cost?
The client sees connection timed out. What do you expect the packet capture on each end to show?

interviewQA.q: What is TIME_WAIT, why does it exist, and when is it actually a problem?
interviewQA.a: TIME_WAIT is entered by whichever side closes the connection first, after it has sent its final ACK, and it lasts 2*MSL - on Linux a hardcoded 60 seconds in TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN, which notably is not a sysctl. It exists for two reasons. One, delayed duplicate segments from the old connection may still be wandering the network, and if a new connection reused the same four-tuple immediately, those stragglers could be accepted as valid data. Two, if the peer's final FIN is retransmitted because our last ACK was lost, we must still be around to re-acknowledge it, otherwise the peer gets an RST and its close looks like an error. On a server, TIME_WAIT sockets are usually harmless - they hold minimal state, and a well-behaved server is not typically the side that closes. Where it bites is on a client or a proxy making many short-lived outbound connections, because each TIME_WAIT holds an ephemeral port for that destination tuple. With the default port range of 32768-60999 you have around 28,000 ports toward a single destination IP and port, which at 60 seconds each caps you around 470 new connections per second to one backend. The right fix is almost always to stop creating connections - HTTP keep-alive and a properly sized connection pool - and secondarily to add destinations or enable tcp_tw_reuse for outbound sockets. The fix I would never recommend is tcp_tw_recycle: it broke clients behind NAT because it made per-host timestamp assumptions, and it was removed from the kernel in 4.12.
followUps: Which sysctl controls FIN_WAIT_2, and why do people confuse it with TIME_WAIT?
You see 40,000 TIME_WAIT sockets on a web server. Is that a problem? How would you decide?
How would you compute the maximum sustainable rate of new connections to one backend?

interviewQA.q: A service accumulates tens of thousands of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT. What is happening and how do you fix it?
interviewQA.a: CLOSE_WAIT means the remote peer sent a FIN and our kernel acknowledged it, and now the socket is waiting for our application to call close on the file descriptor. The kernel cannot advance the state machine for us - only the application can decide it is done writing. So a growing CLOSE_WAIT count is never a network fault; it is a resource leak in our code. Typically it is a client library or a connection pool where responses are read but the connection object is dropped without being closed, or an error path that returns early without a defer or finally, or a pool whose eviction never actually closes evicted entries. The consequence is file-descriptor exhaustion, which surfaces later as accept failures, inability to open files, or an EMFILE crash - usually far from the real cause. To diagnose: ss -tanp state close-wait gives me the owning process and the peer addresses, which tells me which dependency's connections are leaking; lsof or the count in /proc/PID/fd confirms fd growth over time. The fix is in the code. As a stopgap I would raise the fd limit and restart on a schedule, but I would be explicit that that is buying time, not fixing anything.
followUps: How would you distinguish this from FIN_WAIT_2 accumulation, and what does that one mean?
What monitoring would have caught this before it caused an outage?
Could a load balancer's idle timeout produce this pattern?

interviewQA.q: Explain the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer, and how you would choose.
interviewQA.a: An L4 load balancer decides using only transport headers - the five-tuple of source and destination address and port plus protocol. It picks a backend when the connection is established and then forwards every packet of that flow to the same place using a flow table. Because it never parses the payload it works for any TCP or UDP protocol, adds microseconds of latency, scales horizontally with ECMP and consistent hashing, and can pass TLS straight through so it never holds a private key. An L7 load balancer terminates the connection, parses HTTP, and decides per request. That buys routing by host and path, header manipulation including X-Forwarded-For, per-request retries and timeouts, canary splits by weight or header, response caching and compression, and centralised TLS termination. It costs more per request, requires decryption to be useful, and is protocol-specific. My default is L7 for HTTP APIs and web traffic, and L4 for databases, brokers, arbitrary TCP, and cases where compliance requires no decryption point. The important subtlety is HTTP/2 and gRPC: they multiplex thousands of requests over one long-lived connection, so an L4 balancer that chooses a backend per connection pins all of that traffic to one pod, and after a scale-up the new pods get nothing. For gRPC I want either an L7 proxy that balances per request, or client-side load balancing over a headless service, or a max-connection-age on the server so pools reshuffle periodically.
followUps: How does the load balancer keep a flow going to the same backend at L4, and what happens when the backend set changes?
Why is least-outstanding-requests usually better than round robin?
How would you preserve the client's source IP through each of the two designs?

interviewQA.q: dig resolves a hostname correctly but the application says it cannot resolve it. How is that possible, and how do you debug it?
interviewQA.a: Because they use different code paths. dig and nslookup talk directly to a nameserver over the DNS protocol. An application calling getaddrinfo goes through NSS, the Name Service Switch, whose sources and order are configured in /etc/nsswitch.conf - typically files then dns, meaning /etc/hosts is consulted first and can override DNS entirely. Between those, systemd-resolved may be interposing with its own per-link configuration and cache. So the disagreement is itself the diagnosis, and the correct tool for what the application will actually see is getent hosts, or getent ahosts if I care about both address families. The usual causes are a stale or wrong entry in /etc/hosts, a container whose /etc/resolv.conf points at a nameserver it cannot reach, an nsswitch line missing dns, or search-domain behaviour - a short name that resolves on one host because of its search list and not on another. In Kubernetes I would also check ndots: with the default ndots:5 an external name is tried against every search domain first, so an intermittent failure can come from CoreDNS pressure rather than from the record. And I would check whether the application caches: JVMs historically cached resolutions for the process lifetime, and many connection pools resolve once at startup, so an application can be wrong about DNS long after DNS is right.
followUps: What is the difference between NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, and NOERROR with an empty answer?
How do you check whether the local resolver is stale versus the authoritative record being wrong?
Why is DNS-based failover unreliable, and what would you use instead?

interviewQA.q: Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. What problem does each version solve?
interviewQA.a: HTTP/1.1's defining constraint is that one connection carries one request at a time. Pipelining was specified but responses must return in order, so a slow response blocks everything behind it - application-level head-of-line blocking - and browsers worked around it by opening up to six connections per origin, which is why domain sharding used to be a performance technique. HTTP/2 keeps the semantics and replaces the wire format with binary frames carrying stream identifiers, so many exchanges interleave over one connection. It adds HPACK header compression, which matters because headers are large and repetitive, and per-stream flow control. That removes HTTP's head-of-line blocking, but not TCP's: every stream shares one ordered byte stream, so one lost packet stalls delivery of all streams until it is retransmitted. On a clean datacentre link that is irrelevant; on a lossy mobile path HTTP/2 can be worse than six independent connections. HTTP/3 fixes that by running over QUIC on UDP, where streams are a transport concept and loss on one does not block the others. QUIC also integrates TLS 1.3 into the transport handshake so a fresh connection is one round trip and a resumed one can be zero, and it identifies connections by a connection ID rather than the four-tuple, so a client changing network keeps the same connection. The deployment realities I would mention: negotiation is by ALPN inside TLS for h2, and out of band via Alt-Svc or an HTTPS DNS record for h3 since it is a different transport; some networks block UDP/443 so clients keep a TCP fallback; and server push, which people still bring up, was removed from Chrome in 2022 in favour of 103 Early Hints.
